## 1. Direct Answer
- AT&T’s planned spectrum and fiber purchases are expected to lift net leverage roughly to the 3x area next year (Bloomberg Intelligence: “AT&T expects net leverage to increase to about 3x next year with the acquisitions of Lumen's consumer fiber business and spectrum from EchoStar”) [2][6].  
- Bloomberg Intelligence also projects net leverage will likely increase to about 3.2x with the EchoStar spectrum purchase (“net leverage will likely increase to about 3.2x with the EchoStar spectrum purchase”) [1].  
- JPMorgan’s credit work expects leverage to rise to the “3.6x-3.7x range in 2026” after the EchoStar acquisition, before improving later (“our expectation that AT&T's leverage will increase to the 3.6x-3.7x range in 2026”) [4].  
- Several research notes flag a potential funding gap and additional borrowing needs: analysts point to a roughly $10 billion net shortfall through 2026 that could prompt new debt issuance, and that AT&T “may borrow to help fund” material deal and reward outlays [6][3].  
- The company faces multi‑year debt‑maturity refinancing needs—reports cite roughly $5–8 billion of annual maturities for 2027–36 and $5–10 billion of annual maturities in the coming years—implying a need to refinance much of its obligations (“AT&T faces $5-8 billion of annual maturities for 2027-36”) [1][6].  
- Elevated shareholder returns (annual dividend payments of $7–8 billion and about $8 billion of average yearly share repurchases for 2026–28) and large acquisitions could constrain free cash flow available to reduce debt, increasing reliance on bond markets (“about $9 billion of cash flow will likely be used to fund shareholder rewards”; “annual dividend payments of $7-$8 billion and … about $8 billion of average yearly share repurchases for 2026-28”) [1][5].  
- Market and rating risks: analysts note AT&T bonds trade at wider spreads than peers, which can raise financing costs (“AT&T bonds (Baa2/BBB/BBB+) trade at spreads that are wider than notes issued by peers”) [2][3].  
- Rating agencies have reacted to the spectrum deal; Fitch placed its BBB+ rating on rating‑watch negative and “could lower its ranking to BBB,” and S&P moved to neutral from positive—indicating near‑term downgrade risk tied to the deal and leverage path (“Fitch on Aug. 28 placed its BBB+ rating for AT&T on rating watch-negative … could lower its ranking to BBB”; “S&P affirmed its BBB rating, yet changed its outlook to neutral from positive”) [1][6].  
- JPMorgan summarizes explicit downgrade triggers: ratings could be downgraded if leverage “rises above 4x on a sustained basis” or if “debt/EBITDA is expected to be sustained above 3.5x and free cash flow as a percentage of debt turns negative for an extended period” [4].  
- Morningstar reports net debt of $118 billion at end‑2025 and notes AT&T expects net leverage to “tick back up to 3.0 times EBITDA at the end of 2026, requiring up to three years to return to its target level,” highlighting the multi‑year horizon to repair credit metrics after the transactions (“Net debt stood at $118 billion at the end of 2025 … net leverage at about 2.5 times EBITDA”; “AT&T expects net debt leverage to tick back up to 3.0 times EBITDA at the end of 2026, requiring up to three years to return to its target level”) [8].
